label: Chapter 2: The House of Luxembourg, 963 to 1443

units.text: For its first two centuries, Siegfried's county was a modest affair.
It was a rocky fortress, a handful of villages, and a dynasty that married well and waited.
The counts of Luxembourg slowly gathered land, and in 1136 a stroke of inheritance gave the county to Henry the Blind, count of Namur, who joined the two territories together.
His daughter became one of the most remarkable rulers in the story.
Her name was Ermesinde. She inherited the county in 1196 and ruled for more than fifty years, through two marriages and a great deal of politics.
Ermesinde is remembered for granting charters of freedom to the towns of her county.
In 1244, she gave one to the city of Luxembourg, and it freed its townspeople from many of the old obligations of serfdom and let them organize themselves as a community, with a council of their own.
In a Europe where most people lived under their lord's thumb, that was a bold step.
To this day, Luxembourg treats Ermesinde as one of its founding figures.
Now we reach the part of the story where this small county suddenly leaps onto the continental stage.
In 1288, the count of Luxembourg was killed at the Battle of Worringen, in a war over the succession to the neighboring duchy of Limburg.
His heir was a boy of about thirteen, also named Henry.
We know him as Henry the Seventh.
As a young man, he was widely admired.
He was said to be chivalrous, pious, and quietly ambitious.
And in 1308, after the German king was murdered, the electors of the empire looked around for someone who was capable but not too powerful.
They chose the count of Luxembourg.
That is an astonishing moment.
A lord from a small county on the western edge of the empire suddenly found himself king of the Germans.
And Henry seized the chance. He arranged for his teenage son John to marry Elisabeth, the heiress of the kingdom of Bohemia, which is roughly today's Czech Republic.
John became King of Bohemia in 1310.
In one stroke, the House of Luxembourg had acquired one of the richest crowns in central Europe.
Henry himself marched over the Alps into Italy, where he was crowned emperor in Rome in 1312.
He dreamed of restoring imperial glory.
The poet Dante, who lived through those years and pinned his hopes on Henry, wrote that a seat was waiting for him in Paradise.
But Henry died of a fever in 1313, near the city of Siena, and the dream died with him.
His son John had a very different life.
Known to history as John the Blind, he was one of the great adventurers of the Middle Ages.
He was born in Luxembourg and raised partly at the French court.
As King of Bohemia, he was almost never home.
He fought in Italy, in Poland, and in Lithuania, alongside the crusading Teutonic Knights.
He loved tournaments, and he loved France.
His daughter Bonne married the man who would become King John the Second of France, and she became the grandmother of a future French king.
By around 1340, John had lost his sight completely.
It did not slow him down. In 1340 he founded a fair in Luxembourg City that still exists today, the Schueberfouer.
It takes place every year in late August and early September, with rides, food stalls, and traditional parades, and it is the biggest funfair in the country.
Then came the war that would define his end.
In 1346, England and France were fighting what we now call the Hundred Years' War, and John, loyal to the French, rode to the battlefield of Crécy.
Blind, he asked his knights to lead him into the fight.
According to the old account, they tied their horses together by the reins, so that he would not be separated, and charged straight into the English archers.
By the next morning, John and his companions were found dead on the field.
Tradition says that the English prince, the one we call the Black Prince, who was just sixteen, took the three ostrich feathers from John's helmet as a trophy, and made them his own emblem.
Historians argue about whether that is really true.
But in Luxembourg, John is remembered as the great national hero.
His body now rests in the crypt of Notre-Dame cathedral in the capital, and to Luxembourgers he is a symbol of bravery, loyalty, and a certain doomed gallantry.
We come now to the greatest of the Luxembourgers.
John's eldest son was born in Prague and baptized with the name Wenceslas, but he took the name Charles at the French court, in honor of his godfather and uncle.
As Charles the Fourth, he became King of Bohemia after his father's death, and in 1355 he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome.
Charles was a very different kind of emperor from his father and grandfather.
He was a scholar, a builder, and a patient politician.
In 1356 he issued a famous decree called the Golden Bull, which fixed how emperors would be elected by seven electors, a system that more or less lasted until the empire itself ended.
He founded Charles University in Prague in 1348, the first university in central Europe.
He started building the stone bridge across the Vltava that still bears his name.
He turned Prague into one of the great cities of Europe.
And he did not forget the little county where his family began.
In 1354, Charles raised Luxembourg to the rank of duchy, and installed his half-brother Wenceslas as its first duke.
So by the late fourteenth century, the House of Luxembourg was one of the great dynasties of Europe.
Its sons ruled Bohemia, and for a time Hungary, and sat on the imperial throne.
In all, four Luxembourgers held the title of ruler of the Holy Roman Empire: Henry the Seventh, Charles the Fourth, Charles's son Wenceslas the Fourth, and Charles's other son Sigismund.
Only three of them, Henry, Charles and Sigismund, were actually crowned emperor in Rome.
Sigismund was the last. A shrewd and restless man, he was King of Hungary from 1387, and he became King of the Romans in 1411.

He called the great Council of Constance, which met from 1414 to 1418 and ended a split in the Catholic Church, and which also burned the Czech reformer Jan Hus, an act that triggered the Hussite wars in Bohemia.
Sigismund was crowned emperor in 1433, and he died in 1437.
He had no surviving son. With his death, the male line of the House of Luxembourg came to an end.
Notice what happened to the little duchy of Luxembourg through all this.
Its glamorous rulers were scattered across central Europe.
They spent most of their time in Prague, Buda or Rome, and they rarely visited the place that had made them.
To them, Luxembourg was a source of money, and they treated it that way.
They mortgaged it. They pledged it as security for loans, and passed it around among cousins and creditors.
One of the people who ended up holding it was a woman named Elisabeth of Görlitz, a niece of Sigismund.
She was widowed, remarried, and constantly short of money.
In the end, she sold her rights to the most powerful figure in the region: Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.
In 1443, his forces took possession of the city, reportedly by a surprise assault with the help of local nobles who were fed up with the unstable rule of the pledge-holders.
And just like that, the old era came to an end.
The county that had given Europe emperors and kings was now just one more piece in the growing Burgundian collection of lands.
Before we move on, one more thread worth remembering.
In the countryside of Luxembourg, medieval lords built castles that still stand.
The most spectacular is Vianden, on a hill above a river in the north, one of the largest feudal residences in this part of Europe.
In the early fifteenth century, Vianden passed by inheritance to the family of Nassau, which would later become the Dutch royal house.
Keep that name in mind. Four hundred years later, it will be central to our story.
Next, we enter the age of the fortress.
